scope: local-only; no AWS writes; not browser Apply/Save/Reload proof

results.summary: The platform architecture strongly covers detection, coordinated remediation, rollback, learning, and auditability, but the 5-minute remediation constraint is not explicitly enforced end-to-end.

findings.title: End-to-end remediation SLA is not explicitly enforced
findings.explanation: The design includes deadlines, short-lived permits, and bounded execution steps, but it does not explicitly define or enforce a 5-minute budget from anomaly detection to completed remediation. That leaves the timing constraint dependent on implementation choices rather than architecture, which can jeopardize the published auto-remediation deadline.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit incident-level SLA budget that is decomposed across detection, correlation, policy approval, queueing, execution, and verification, with hard timeouts and priority handling tied to the 5-minute constraint.

results.summary: The design covers the core capacity-planning workflow well, including forecasting, scenario modeling, rightsizing, leadership reporting, multi-cloud views, and capacity alerts, but it lacks explicit enforcement of the 90-day accuracy target and clearer degraded-mode handling for missing provider data.

findings.title: Accuracy target is modeled but not explicitly enforced
findings.explanation: The architecture has the right ingredients for forecast evaluation, but it does not show an explicit control that rejects or flags models that miss the 10% error requirement over the 90-day horizon. Without a thresholded backtest or acceptance gate, the constraint is only partially addressed.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit evaluation gate in the forecasting pipeline or monitoring workflow that compares 90-day backtests against the 10% target and blocks promotion of noncompliant model versions.

findings.title: Failure handling for partial provider data could still leave stale forecasts
findings.explanation: The queue and collector correctly distinguish partial-source status from zero usage, but the design does not explicitly describe how stale or missing provider slices are isolated from downstream forecast generation when a provider remains unavailable. That leaves a reliability gap for multi-cloud completeness under collection failures.
findings.recommendation: Define stale-data handling rules in the forecaster and optimizer, such as source-level freshness cutoffs, degraded-mode forecasting, and explicit exclusion or weighting of missing provider slices.

results.summary: The design covers the full change-risk workflow end to end, including correlation, scoring, blast-radius analysis, deployment-window recommendation, policy enforcement, and CI/CD/change-management integration; one policy precedence detail remains open.

findings.title: Policy precedence for conflicting maintenance-window and risk signals is not fully specified
findings.explanation: The architecture supports maintenance windows, risk scores, blast radius, and source approval reconciliation, but it does not state how the policy engine resolves conflicts when the proposed deployment window is outside the allowed window yet the change is otherwise low risk. That leaves an implementation decision open for the approval path and could affect consistent enforcement.
findings.recommendation: Define a deterministic policy precedence order for risk, maintenance windows, collision checks, and source approval state, including whether any of these conditions can be waived for auto-approval.

results.summary: The design cleanly covers real-time SLI/SLO monitoring, continuous error-budget computation, 1–4 hour breach forecasting, confidence-based alerting, composite SLAs, and customer reporting with a coherent streaming control/reporting split.

findings.title: Clear separation of ingestion, evaluation, forecasting, and reporting
findings.explanation: The design isolates telemetry collection, SLO definition management, budget computation, forecasting, mitigation, and customer reporting into distinct components with explicit flows between them. That separation reduces coupling and makes the SLA lifecycle easier to operate and evolve.

findings.title: Composite SLA and multi-window budget support are modeled explicitly
findings.explanation: The registry carries service-chain composition and the evaluator computes hourly, daily, and monthly budgets, which directly matches the composite and multi-window scope without requiring extra components.

results.summary: The design presents a coherent chaos-engineering control loop with governed execution, safety gating, real-time monitoring, ML-based experiment selection, and evidence-backed scorecards for both operators and CI/CD.

findings.title: Well-partitioned safety and execution flow
findings.explanation: The architecture separates request ingress, policy enforcement, scheduling, execution, monitoring, and analytics. This makes the experiment lifecycle easy to reason about and supports safe operation in production.

findings.title: ML recommendation loop is grounded in reviewed evidence
findings.explanation: Recommendation training uses reviewed resilience evidence and the recommender returns ranked hypotheses with rationale, uncertainty, and provenance, which is a credible control loop for selecting higher-value experiments.

findings.title: Scorecards and analytics are evidence-rich
findings.explanation: The analytics and scorecard layers expose methodology, confidence, limitations, and service-level summaries rather than only raw experiment logs, which supports operator understanding and CI/CD consumption.

results.summary: A coherent multi-cloud FinOps platform with provider-specific ingestion, canonical normalization, allocation-aware analytics, ML-driven anomaly/rightsize/forecast workflows, and governed automated actions.

findings.title: Multi-cloud cost optimization workflow is end-to-end
findings.explanation: The submission covers the full requested workflow: provider ingestion, normalization, allocation, anomaly detection, rightsizing, commitment optimization, forecasting, and policy enforcement. The flows are coherent and match the published core scope.

findings.title: Governance and auditability are well integrated
findings.explanation: The design preserves versioned policies, approval records, audit references, and lineage from ingestion through optimization and downstream policy evaluation, which supports reviewable FinOps actions.

results.summary: A coherent AIOps observability platform with scalable ingestion, hybrid telemetry handling, topology discovery, cross-signal correlation, natural-language querying, proactive analytics, dashboards, and hot/cold retention support.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end observability pipeline with AI-assisted exploration
findings.explanation: The design covers ingestion, normalization, storage, topology discovery, cross-signal correlation, natural-language querying, summaries, proactive analytics, dashboards, and monitoring in a coherent flow.

findings.title: Clear hot/cold retention strategy for large telemetry volumes
findings.explanation: The design separates query stores from a cold archive and defines lifecycle-managed exports, which is a practical fit for the long-retention constraint.

results.summary: The design covers the core e-commerce serverless scope well, with solid order, payment, inventory, and notification flows; the main remaining issues are quantified peak scaling, explicit operational thresholds, and proving the under-1-second cold-start constraint.

findings.title: Concurrency limits are not yet sized for the full 10,000+ user peak
findings.explanation: The design includes quota-aware throttling, callback caps, and measured tuning for WebSocket fanout, but it does not specify concrete capacity settings or scaling policy showing that the live inventory path can sustain the published 10,000+ concurrent-user target during sale bursts without over-throttling legitimate traffic.
findings.recommendation: Define target connection counts, fanout batch sizes, and backpressure thresholds for the WebSocket and fanout path, then validate them against the 10,000+ concurrent-user requirement.

findings.title: Inventory and socket recovery is described, but not fully closed for all missed-update cases
findings.explanation: The design relies on coalescing stale updates and client resync after reconnect, which is reasonable, but it leaves the exact recovery path for missed live inventory messages dependent on client behavior rather than an explicit server-side replay or catch-up policy.
findings.recommendation: Specify a server-driven catch-up path for missed inventory versions and the reconnect/replay conditions that guarantee clients return to authoritative stock state.

findings.title: Cold-start target is strategy-backed but not demonstrated as met
findings.explanation: The design uses lean runtimes and provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive Lambdas, but it explicitly says the <1s claim must be benchmarked and may be enabled only where measured latency requires it. That leaves the published cold-start constraint only partially satisfied in the submitted architecture.
findings.recommendation: State which functions are covered by provisioned concurrency, the validation threshold for each, and the operating policy that keeps cold starts under 1 second during sale windows.

findings.title: Cold-start constraint compliance is not fully closed
findings.explanation: Because the design conditions compliance on future benchmarking and selective warm capacity, it does not yet show that the architecture satisfies the published under-1-second constraint across the latency-critical request paths.
findings.recommendation: Document the exact cold-start mitigation plan per function, including measured p95/p99 init times and the threshold for enabling provisioned concurrency.

findings.title: Monitoring coverage is broad but not tied to explicit operating thresholds for peak inventory delivery
findings.explanation: The monitoring component lists many relevant signals, yet it does not define concrete alert thresholds or decision points for live inventory lag, active-socket saturation, or fanout backlog during sales events, which limits actionable operational control.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit alert thresholds and runbook triggers for inventory freshness, active socket pressure, and fanout backlog so operators can intervene before user-visible staleness grows.

findings.title: Operational tuning for sale-day capacity is still conditional on measured demand
findings.explanation: Reserved capacity, provisioned concurrency, and quota caps are all described as dependent on benchmarking or measured need, which means the architecture is not yet fully deliverable as a fixed operating plan for the published traffic target.
findings.recommendation: Convert the measured-tuning language into an implementation plan with concrete defaults for sale-day traffic, including initial concurrency reservations and escalation rules.

findings.title: Provisioned concurrency may increase cost without a stated selection policy
findings.explanation: The architecture appropriately uses serverless and on-demand capacity, but it also introduces selective provisioned concurrency without defining when it is enabled or disabled. That leaves the cost posture for variable traffic incomplete, especially for sale windows versus off-peak periods.
findings.recommendation: Define a policy that enables warm capacity only for the minimum set of latency-critical functions and only during documented traffic windows.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end serverless decomposition
findings.explanation: The design cleanly separates catalog, checkout, payment, notification, and live-update concerns into focused serverless and managed-service components, which improves clarity and operational isolation.

results.summary: The design is strong for multi-region failover, data replication, monitoring, and automated recovery, but it does not yet explain how the active standby and replication approach stays cost-effective.

findings.title: Cost strategy is implied but not articulated
findings.explanation: The architecture correctly includes warm standby, cross-region replication, and a protected backup vault, but it does not explain how these choices are kept cost-effective relative to the constraint. In particular, the submission does not state which parts of the standby stack are scaled down, whether all data needs active cross-region replication, or how retention/lifecycle policy is tuned to control ongoing replication and storage cost.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit cost-control policy: define warm-standby sizing, selective replication/backup scope, retention windows, and any lifecycle rules or tiering used to balance recovery objectives against spend.

results.summary: A coherent AWS streaming architecture covers ingestion, real-time processing, analytics, query serving, replay, retention, dashboarding, and pipeline monitoring with no material core-scope gaps.

findings.title: Strong end-to-end streaming path with replay and query surfaces
findings.explanation: The design coherently connects producers, durable stream buffering, Flink processing, query storage, dashboard serving, replay, and monitoring. This supports the core ingestion, processing, analytics, query, visualization, replay, and health-monitoring scope without obvious contradictions.

findings.title: Robust operational visibility across stream, processor, archive, and query store
findings.explanation: Telemetry is routed into CloudWatch from each major stage, including throughput, lag, checkpoint/recovery, replay status, and freshness. This gives a solid basis for monitoring pipeline health and diagnosing failures.

results.summary: The design covers the batch workflow, dependency handling, interruption recovery, S3-backed state, and monitoring well; remaining open decisions are mainly schedule semantics, workflow mode, and fallback policy.

findings.title: Schedule semantics need owner confirmation
findings.explanation: The scheduler is positioned correctly, but the cadence, timezone, catch-up behavior, and duplicate-start policy are intentionally left open. Those choices affect whether reruns are idempotent and whether missed windows are replayed or skipped.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the schedule cadence, timezone, and duplicate/catch-up policy so the trigger behavior matches the workload owner's expectations.

findings.title: Workflow engine duration/cost mode is undecided
findings.explanation: The design uses AWS Step Functions Standard Workflow, but the notes explicitly say Standard versus Express should be confirmed from duration, execution-history, and cost requirements. That is a real implementation choice, not yet a completed decision.
findings.recommendation: Decide between Standard and Express using expected run duration, history retention needs, and orchestration cost targets.

findings.title: Fallback capacity policy is not fully specified
findings.explanation: The architecture prefers Spot capacity and mentions an explicitly approved less interruption-prone fallback only when the SLA is threatened, but it does not define what that fallback is or the thresholds that trigger it. Without that policy, SLA behavior during repeated interruptions remains partly open.
findings.recommendation: Define the approved fallback capacity type and the trigger conditions for switching to it, including the completion-risk threshold.

results.summary: The design cleanly separates public, application, and database tiers, uses WAF and encrypted paths end-to-end, supports autoscaling and Multi-AZ availability, and provides security-event logging through CloudWatch and CloudTrail.

findings.title: WAF and encrypted request path are well aligned with the public attack surface
findings.explanation: Public browser traffic is filtered by AWS WAF before reaching the load balancer, and the path is described as HTTPS throughout the public edge and into the private tiers. This directly addresses the common web-attack and encrypted-transit requirements.

findings.title: Private-tier segmentation supports clear trust boundaries
findings.explanation: The design separates public entry components from private web and database subnets, and the database is reachable only from the application tier. That is a strong network-isolation pattern for this scope.

findings.title: Security telemetry is broadly covered across edge, app, data and audit sources
findings.explanation: CloudWatch receives WAF logs, application security events, database security/connection events, and CloudTrail audit events, giving the design multiple security-event sources rather than a single logging point.
